headline: Widest thermal edge of the season lights up yellowfin on the Hudson's 100-fathom line
subhead: A post-blow warm seam from Wilmington to Poor Man's put fish on the wall this week — here's where to find them before the new moon shuts the light down.
body_markdown:
The blow that sat on us through the holiday weekend finally cleared out Tuesday night, and what it left behind on the shelf edge was worth the wait. By Wednesday morning I was looking at a 10.3-degree differential between the cold shelf water and the warm slope water pushing up against it — the widest thermal split I've seen all season. That's not a subtle seam. That's a wall you could practically see from the tower. The warm plume ran the corridor from Wilmington up through Poor Man's and pressed right into the Hudson's east wall, and where warm water gets shoved up against cold that hard, bait gets pinned and tuna get stupid. Wednesday and Thursday were the first real post-blow window of July, and it produced.

Looking at what's coming, the moon's going dark — we're sliding into new moon territory over the weekend, which means less light penetration at night and a different game for the bluefin crowd working the midshore breaks. The NE upwelling that's been running has sharpened up the 20 to 30 fathom contours nicely, and the Coimbra corridor at 20 fathoms has bluefin stacked on it right now. Darkening moon plus squid on the meter is exactly the setup you want for overnight light-and-jig work — the squid come up in the dark, the bluefin follow, and you don't need much current to make it happen. That's where I'd point a boat this weekend if the canyon run isn't in the cards.

As for the canyon itself, Wednesday's bite was legitimate — not a slaughter, but real fish on real structure. We worked the temp break running along the 100-fathom curve on the east wall, trolling a spread of ballyhoo behind Ilanders — green/yellow and pink/white doing the damage — with a naked ballyhoo flat-lined down the middle. Yellowfin from 35 to low 60s, mixed in with a couple of chunkier fish that felt closer to 70 when they came tight. Nothing giant, but a solid morning bite that shut off hard by early afternoon once the sun got up on the water and the fish slid back down. If you're running out, get there for first light — that window from dawn to about 10 a.m. is where the temp break was actually holding fish, and by midday it went quiet enough that a few boats picked up and ran further east looking for green water and didn't find much better.

Bigeye have been mixed in with the yellowfin on the same water, mostly picked off on the night drift with squid strips or whole squid soaked deep off a downrigger, 250 to 300 feet, right along that same east wall contour. It's not a bigeye blitz — more a fish or two a trip for boats willing to put in a night on anchor or drift over the deeper structure — but the numbers are there for anyone patient enough to sit on it.

Mahi have been scattered but present, mostly picked up incidentally trolling the canyon edge where any bit of floating structure or a weedline held them. Small stuff mostly, schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range, though a few boats found a better grade under a bigger mat of sargassum out past the Dip. If you see color change or a weedline holding out there, it's worth a few casts with a small stickbait or a bucktail before you move on — dolphin don't need much invitation this time of year when the water's this warm.

Wahoo have been quieter than I'd like for mid-July, but the ones that showed came off high-speed trolled Yo-Zuri Bonito lures and cedar plugs run wide on the spread, mostly picked off along the same warm seam on the east wall in that 68 to 70-degree slot where the wahoo like to sit just under the surface temp break. One or two fish a trip for the boats that specifically rigged for them — this isn't a target-and-fill-the-box fishery right now, it's an opportunistic add-on while you're trolling for yellowfin.

White marlin are still a watch-and-wait situation. The warm plume that's been driving this whole week's action is the same signal that typically pushes marlin up onto the bank, and if that plume holds its ground or pushes further west over the next week to ten days, I'd expect the first real flag reports out of the mid-Atlantic canyons, us included. It hasn't happened yet — I haven't heard a confirmed white bite anywhere close to the Hudson this week — but the water's setting up for it, and I'd have a pitch bait rigged and ready if you're running out there regardless of target species.

If I had a boat this weekend, I'd split the difference: run out early for the dawn bite on the east wall temp break while it's producing, and if that shuts down by midday, I'd rather burn the fuel checking the Coimbra corridor at night under the dark moon than keep grinding dead water in daylight. The bluefin bite there has the better odds right now, and the squid-light program under a black sky is about as reliable a setup as this time of year offers. Either way, that shelf-slope edge isn't going to hold this wide forever — if you've got a window this week, I wouldn't sit on it too long.
